title: 1 Samuel 27:1–7
context: Still hunted by Saul, David despairs of safety in Israel and takes his six hundred men and their households to Achish of Gath, who gives him Ziklag. He lives in Philistine country for a year and four months.

verses.text: David said in his heart, “I will now perish one day by the hand of Saul. There is nothing better for me than that I should escape into the land of the Philistines; and Saul will despair of me, to seek me any more in all the borders of Israel. So I will escape out of his hand.”
verses.arminianNotes: David says in his heart, “I will now perish one day by the hand of Saul.” Arminian readers see a weary man whose fear briefly crowds out the promises God had already given him about the kingdom.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see discouragement in a chosen servant, since David had been anointed in chapter 16. Readers in both traditions often note that the narrator records David’s reasoning without saying he consulted the LORD.

verses.text: David arose and passed over, he and the six hundred men who were with him, to Achish the son of Maoch, king of Gath.
verses.arminianNotes: David and his six hundred men cross over to Achish, king of Gath. Arminian readers see a costly decision to seek safety among Israel’s enemies, which brings moral pressures in the chapters that follow.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see David taking refuge in Philistine territory. The narrative lets the tension stand: God’s anointed future king now serves a Philistine ruler while God’s purposes still move forward.

verses.text: David lived with Achish at Gath, he and his men, every man with his household, even David with his two wives, Ahinoam the Jezreelitess and Abigail the Carmelitess, Nabal’s wife.
verses.arminianNotes: David lives at Gath with his men, their households, and his wives Ahinoam and Abigail. Arminian readers see the scale of David’s responsibility, since many families depend on his choices.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see a large community following David into exile. The mention of Abigail, “Nabal’s wife,” recalls chapter 25 and the providential way she joined David’s household.

verses.text: Saul was told that David had fled to Gath, so he stopped looking for him.
verses.arminianNotes: Saul hears that David has fled to Gath and stops looking for him. Arminian readers see David’s plan succeeding on its own terms, though the narrative will soon show what it costs him.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see the pursuit ending as David expected. Readers in both traditions can note that a human plan may achieve its goal while still raising questions the story does not immediately answer.

verses.text: David said to Achish, “If now I have found favor in your eyes, let them give me a place in one of the cities in the country, that I may dwell there. For why should your servant dwell in the royal city with you?”
verses.arminianNotes: David asks Achish, “let them give me a place in one of the cities in the country.” Arminian readers see a prudent request that gives David room to act away from the Philistine king’s close watch.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see David gaining independence through a carefully framed request. His humble words, “why should your servant dwell in the royal city with you?”, also serve his practical purposes.

verses.text: Then Achish gave him Ziklag that day: therefore Ziklag belongs to the kings of Judah to this day.
verses.arminianNotes: Achish gives David Ziklag, which “belongs to the kings of Judah to this day.” Arminian readers see an unexpected gift from a foreign king that later becomes part of Judah’s royal holdings.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see God’s providence working even through a Philistine ruler’s decision. The narrator’s note “to this day” connects the episode to the later history of David’s dynasty.

verses.text: The number of the days that David lived in the country of the Philistines was a full year and four months.
verses.arminianNotes: David stays in Philistine country “a full year and four months.” Arminian readers see a long season in which David lives in a morally complicated place while waiting for God’s timing.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see an extended period of exile before the promised kingdom arrives. The precise length underlines that God’s promises can involve long waiting through uncertain circumstances.
